clue.text: Not known in bar? Then put about "I'm broke"

indicators.note: the abbreviation for not known goes inside the word for a bar

parts.note: taken as written
NK is the form-filling abbreviation for not known

indicators.note: put about means the three letters of put are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker unknown at the pub turns round and confesses to having no money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' gives UPT, and 'in' signals the container. 'I'm' only lets the clue end as a cry of despair.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flat broke has no money at all, which is what being declared insolvent amounts to.

clue.text: Our Wednesday, or a godlike "duck noise" joke

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, the letter O
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A whimsical remark about a godlike deity and the quacking of a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: Wednesday is Woden's day, and Woden is the Old English form of the chief Norse god; 'or a godlike' and 'joke' are surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Wednesday takes its English name from Woden, the Germanic form of the Norse chief god, so the god is in our weekday's name.

clue.text: Perhaps grey mould in Humpty Dumpty's lair

parts.note: EG, for example, is a way of saying perhaps

indicators.note: to mould is to shape something anew, so the letters of grey are reshaped

explanation.surface: Grey mould may be found where the nursery-rhyme egg Humpty Dumpty lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mould' looks like a noun after 'grey', the colour of mould, but it is the anagram signal, giving GERY.
explanation.definitionFit: An eggery is a place where eggs are kept, a fitting home for the egg-shaped nursery-rhyme figure.

clue.text: Determined spirit name of Jules must bear

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so the deity holds the novelist's surname inside

parts.note: a god is a divine spirit
Jules Verne, the French novelist

explanation.surface: A determined spirit has to carry the name of the novelist Jules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must bear' signals the container; 'spirit' tempts towards drink or ghosts, but here it is a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing that is governed is controlled or decided, so determined is a synonym in that sense.

clue.text: To kiss needs courage in this traffic jam

parts.note: bottle is British slang for nerve or courage
to neck is to kiss and cuddle

explanation.surface: It takes nerve to snog someone while stuck in a traffic jam.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the kissing first but the courage comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottleneck is a narrow point where traffic is held up, so it describes a jam of vehicles.

clue.text: "To waste away" averts my anagram

indicators.note: the setter openly says the letters of averts are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The clue cheerfully admits that one word is a rearrangement of another.
explanation.definitionFit: To starve is to waste away from lack of food.

clue.text: Dresses with straps that are about to fade

indicators.note: the straps are said to go around, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: bands are straps
to age is to fade or grow old

explanation.surface: Clothes with straps that are starting to lose their colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses' looks like a noun for clothes; it is the verb, as when a nurse dresses a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress a wound is to cover it, so bandages is the verb in that sense.

clue.text: Tessa and I curled up to have a nap

indicators.note: curling up twists the letters of the two names into a new order

explanation.surface: Two people curl up together for an afternoon doze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' only joins the two pieces of fodder; it adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short sleep taken in the afternoon, a nap.

clue.text: Loves to scoff wine in place where it is made

indicators.note: to scoff is to gobble food, so the two loves swallow the wine

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, so two loves are two letters O
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Lovers tuck into wine in the very town where it is produced.
explanation.walkthrough: Port wine takes its name from the Portuguese city, so 'it' in the definition refers back to the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is shipped from the Portuguese city of that name, so the city is where the wine is made.

clue.text: Here you will see a second family hide

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: A second family turns up in a concealed place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hide' looks like a verb meaning conceal; it is the noun, an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hide is the skin of an animal, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: How school of Sherlock Holmes is classified

definitions.text: How school of Sherlock Holmes is classified

parts.words: How school of Sherlock Holmes is classified
parts.note: a primary school has the same label as the detective's famous word to Watson, dismissing a deduction as simple

explanation.surface: A question about which category of school the great detective attended.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes's catchphrase to Watson is linked with the term for a primary school.
explanation.definitionFit: A primary school is so called, and the word is the one the fictional detective uses for an easy deduction.

clue.text: "Fancy a massage, backwards", Fanny meant

indicators.note: the whole phrase before it is to be read from the end back to the start

parts.note: a yen is a fancy or longing
a rub is a massage

explanation.surface: Someone named Fanny meant to ask for a back massage.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney was an eighteenth-century English novelist; 'meant' just links her first name to the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Frances Burney was known as Fanny, so that first name points to her surname.

clue.text: Important memo to an upright chap

parts.note: a note is a memo
a worthy is a respectable, upstanding person

explanation.surface: An important memo is sent to a respectable gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth noting is remarkable or significant, so important is a synonym.

clue.text: This sympathetic newsman did present

parts.note: tender means gentle and sympathetic
ED, short for editor, is a newspaper man

explanation.surface: A kindly journalist handed something over.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender is to offer or present formally, so the past tense means did present.

clue.text: Marching and music get beneath the skin

definitions.meaning: a military display of marching bands and drill performed as entertainment
to mark the skin permanently with ink pricked in

explanation.surface: Military bands parade and the sound gets under one's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A military display is called by this name, and the same word is the verb for inking a design into skin.

clue.text: "One drink", said outside, "but it must be new"

indicators.note: the word for spoken goes around the outside of the other pieces

parts.note: oral means spoken or said
I is the Roman numeral one
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone orders one drink, insisting it be a new one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' signals the container; 'said' reads like speech marks in the surface but stands for spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Something original is new and not copied, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Most curious bent toes — daughters must come in!

indicators.note: the daughters are told to come inside, so they are placed within the other letters
bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters of toes are rearranged

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter, doubled for daughters

explanation.surface: Strangely bent toes, and the daughters have to come indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' gives OEST, and 'must come in' signals the container; the dash makes the daughters look like a separate exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The oddest thing is the strangest, so it means most curious.

clue.text: A house divided must keep men in view

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the belief contains the men

parts.note: a tenet is a held view or belief
taken as written

explanation.surface: A house split in two must keep its men in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must keep' signals the container; 'in view' reads as one phrase in the surface, but 'in' is only a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a building divided into separate flats, a house split into dwellings.

clue.text: Has time, when taking silver, to be shocked

indicators.note: taking silver means adding it on, here at the front

parts.note: AG is the chemical symbol for silver
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has time on their hands but is stunned on receiving silver.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means filled with horror, so it is a synonym for shocked.

clue.text: Doctor confessing, getting very wet!

parts.note: owning up is confessing, so owning means confessing

explanation.surface: A doctor admits something while getting soaked.
explanation.definitionFit: Drowning is being submerged in water, the extreme of getting very wet.

clue.text: Sailor's fund-raiser keeps the money locked

indicators.note: to keep is to hold, so the fund-raiser holds the money inside
the money is shut away inside, confirming it goes within

parts.note: a rag is a British student charity fund-raising event
tin is slang for money

explanation.surface: A sailor's charity collection keeps its takings under lock and key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' and 'locked' signal the container. A RAG is a British university charity event; 'Sailor's' is read as sailor is.
explanation.definitionFit: A rating is a non-commissioned sailor in the Royal Navy; the 's stands for is.

clue.text: As head of state, petitioning he'll get

parts.note: taken as written
a king is a head of state

explanation.surface: A head of state is given what he petitions for.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking means requesting, the same as petitioning.

clue.text: As Wren rebuilt, you need to take the blame

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the letters of the architect's name and As into a new structure

explanation.surface: Christopher Wren, the London architect, must answer for a rebuilt building.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral in London; 'rebuilt' fits his trade.
explanation.definitionFit: To answer for something is to be held responsible, so the word means take the blame.

clue.text: So Messrs Grouse wound Mr Stag with pain

indicators.note: wound, from wind, means twisted round, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pair of grouse injure a stag, causing it pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' looks like an injury but is the past tense of wind; the anagram of MRSTAG and PAIN gives all ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: These birds are a kind of grouse of mountain regions, so the plural fits several grouse.

clue.text: Grovelling SM leaves, but troops remain

indicators.note: the letters SM leave, so they are taken away from the word for grovelling

parts.note: smarmy means oily and grovelling

explanation.surface: A sergeant major leaves, but the soldiers stay behind.
explanation.walkthrough: SM is also the abbreviation for sergeant major, which helps the military surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An army is a large body of troops.

clue.text: Help one to form this operatic name

parts.note: aid means help
A is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to help form an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Aida is the title of Verdi's opera and the name of its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Aida is the heroine and title of Verdi's opera.

clue.text: This flowery girl can't reach a thrown-up mound

indicators.note: falling short of the end means the final letter is lost

parts.note: an ant-heap is a mound thrown up by ants

explanation.surface: A girl named after a flower cannot get to the top of a heap of earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthea comes from the Greek for flowery, which is why the girl is 'flowery'.
explanation.definitionFit: The name Anthea comes from the Greek anthos, flower, so it means flowery.

clue.text: Plodding or pirates' noisy cat-like sound

definitions.meaning: walking heavily, putting the feet down
the pirates in Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance sing loudly of moving with catlike steps

explanation.surface: Pirates stamp along making a racket while claiming to be as quiet as cats.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pirates of Penzance the chorus bellows 'With cat-like tread', so their stealthy walk is anything but quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Plodding is walking heavily, and the pirates' song describes their stealthy stepping in the same word.
